title: Airtel Dethroned India's Biggest Private Bank. Here Is What That Tells Us About Where the Money Is Going.
excerpt: Bharti Airtel briefly surpassed HDFC Bank to become India's second most valuable listed company — a ₹12 lakh crore milestone that signals a structural re-rating of Indian telecoms
body:
For the first time in years, India's second most valuable listed company is not a bank. On May 18, Bharti Airtel's market capitalisation touched ₹11.78 lakh crore, edging past HDFC Bank's ₹11.74 lakh crore and leaving only Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries — at roughly ₹18 lakh crore — ahead of it on the Bombay Stock Exchange.

The moment was brief. HDFC Bank clawed back ground by the close. But the symbolism is durable: Dalal Street is telling you, in the only language it speaks, that it believes India's future runs on data more than it runs on deposits.

## A Five-Year Divergence

The numbers are striking. Over the past five years, Airtel shares have surged 270 percent. HDFC Bank, once the consensus pick for the best-managed large company in India, has delivered a comparatively modest 49 percent. In 2026 alone, Airtel is down 8 percent — but HDFC Bank is down 23 percent, battered by a governance crisis that began with the resignation of part-time Chairman Atanu Chakraborty and has since spiralled into broader questions about succession planning at the country's largest private lender.

Airtel shares were trading 2.1 percent higher on the day at ₹1,946.6, near the session's high. HDFC Bank was down 0.4 percent at ₹764.5.

## What the Brokerages Are Saying

The analyst consensus on Airtel is unusually bullish. BofA Securities holds a target price of ₹2,320, calling the risk-reward "firmly in Airtel's favour." The brokerage cited healthy market share gains, momentum in non-cellular business segments and upside from Airtel's growing data centre business.

JP Morgan, targeting ₹2,250 by March 2027, identified three catalysts beyond 5G premiumisation: growth in adjacent businesses, deleveraging and rising dividends. Goldman Sachs retained a Buy rating with a 12-month target of ₹2,210, trimmed from ₹2,250, noting weakness in towers and direct-to-home television.

## Q4 Tells a Nuanced Story

Airtel's March quarter results were credible if uneven. Consolidated revenues and EBITDA came in 1–3 percent ahead of consensus estimates. Africa delivered a standout performance with revenues up 41 percent year-on-year — or 17 percent in constant currency. India's home broadband segment grew 9.5 percent quarter-on-quarter.

India mobile revenues, however, grew just 8 percent year-on-year and 0.6 percent sequentially — a number that suggests tariff hike-led growth is decelerating and the next leg must come from premiumisation and postpaid migration. The company announced a dividend of ₹24 per share for FY26, up from ₹16 in FY25 and ahead of the consensus expectation of ₹20.

In a separate strategic move, Airtel announced a share swap to acquire Indian Continent Investment Ltd's 16.31 percent stake in Airtel Africa, representing approximately 2.4 percent dilution.

## Mittal's 51 Percent Ambition

Bharti Enterprises Chairman Sunil Bharti Mittal outlined a long-term ownership plan, saying he expects Bharti Telecom to regain a controlling 51 percent stake in the business over the next decade, up from slightly over 40 percent currently. Promoter holding stood unchanged at 48.87 percent as of the March 2026 quarter.

## The Diaspora Lens

For NRI investors — a community that has historically favoured banking stocks as a proxy for India's growth story — the Airtel-HDFC Bank swap carries a practical message. Indian telecoms are no longer a value play or a turnaround bet. They are the growth story, powered by 5G rollout, data consumption that continues to climb and an expanding digital economy that needs towers, fibre and data centres before it needs anything else.

The question is whether this re-rating holds. HDFC Bank's fundamentals remain strong — it reported a 10.9 percent net profit increase for the full year — and its governance issues are fixable. But the market is pricing in something deeper than a single quarter or a single chairman's exit. It is pricing in a view about which sectors will define India's next decade. On that question, Airtel's brief moment at number two may prove to be less an anomaly than a preview.
